sections.body_md:
An inner product is a way of multiplying two vectors and getting a scalar, with three rules. It is linear in each argument, symmetric for real vectors, and positive when a nonzero vector is paired with itself. The ordinary dot product is the standard example. The Frobenius product does the same job for matrices: multiply matching entries and add, which is also the trace of \(A^T B\).

The inner product measures angle. Nonzero vectors are orthogonal when the pairing is zero. The cosine of the angle is the inner product divided by the product of the lengths. The length itself is recovered by taking the square root of the inner product of a vector with itself. That length is a norm, and it is the 2-norm when the inner product is the dot product.

Not every bilinear formula works. If a pairing can be negative on a vector with itself, it violates positivity and cannot define a length.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For the dot product, \(\langle x, y \rangle = x^T y\) and \(\lVert x \rVert_2 = \sqrt{x^T x}\). The angle satisfies
\[
\cos\theta = \frac{\langle x, y \rangle}{\lVert x \rVert\,\lVert y \rVert}
\]
when both vectors are nonzero. Orthogonal means \(\langle x, y \rangle = 0\). The Frobenius product is \(\langle A, B \rangle_F = \sum_{ij} a_{ij} b_{ij} = \mathrm{tr}(A^T B)\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
The vectors \((3,2)\) and \((2,-3)\) have dot product 0. They are orthogonal, even though neither is an axis vector. Each has squared length \(9+4 = 13\).

Separately, take
\[
A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The entrywise products are 6, 0, 0, and 2. The Frobenius inner product has value 8. The trace formula \(\mathrm{tr}(A^T B)\) gives the same 8. The product of the two determinants is a different number and is not the inner product.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Orthogonality is not equal length. A positive dot product means an acute angle, not orthogonality. The Frobenius product is not the product of determinants or the product of traces. A formula such as \(x_1 y_1 - x_2 y_2\) is bilinear and symmetric, but it gives a negative square on the second basis vector, so it is not an inner product. The zero vector is orthogonal to everything, and it is excluded when an angle is computed because the lengths in the denominator vanish.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Cauchy-Schwarz says the absolute inner product cannot exceed the product of the lengths, with equality exactly for parallel vectors. Gram-Schmidt uses the coefficient \(\langle v, u \rangle / \langle u, u \rangle\) to subtract the part of \(v\) parallel to \(u\). When the inner product is \(u^T Q v\) for a positive definite \(Q\), that same orthogonality is called conjugacy and is the geometry behind conjugate directions.
